cards.question: Birrell (1989): what is "An Introduction to Programming with Threads"?
cards.answer: A practical tutorial on using fork/join, mutexes, condition variables, and alerts correctly.
cards.memory: Programming-model layer. The model behind pthreads.
distractors: A redesign of the SunOS kernel around kernel threads.
A user-level threads library built on LWPs.
An event-driven web server design.

cards.question: Birrell: name 5 reasons to use threads.
cards.answer: Use multiprocessors, overlap work with slow devices, keep a UI responsive, serve many network clients, and defer work to cut latency.
distractors: Lower memory use, no locks, no scheduling, portability, and security.
Avoid system calls, avoid interrupts, avoid I/O, avoid caches, and avoid IPC.
Replace processes, replace the kernel, replace signals, replace pipes, and replace files.

cards.question: Birrell: what does Fork(proc, arg) return?
cards.answer: A handle to the new thread (later passed to Join).
distractors: The procedure's result.
A new process ID.
Nothing; the thread is anonymous.

cards.question: Birrell: how often is Join used, and why?
cards.answer: Rarely. Most threads are daemons that are never joined.
distractors: After every Fork, or the thread leaks.
Only for threads that hold a mutex.
Never; Birrell's model has no Join.

cards.question: Birrell: what does the LOCK m DO … END clause do?
cards.answer: Locks the mutex, runs the statements, then unlocks automatically.
cards.memory: Holding the mutex is the only way to touch its data: a monitor.
distractors: Locks the mutex until the thread exits.
Runs the statements only if the mutex is free, otherwise skips them.
Disables interrupts while the statements run.

cards.question: Birrell: what does Wait(m, c) do atomically?
cards.answer: Unlocks m and blocks on c in one step (then re-locks m on wake-up).
distractors: Locks m and signals c in one step.
Blocks on c while keeping m locked.
Unlocks m, then checks c once without blocking.

cards.question: Why must Wait's unlock-and-block be atomic?
cards.answer: Otherwise a Signal could arrive between the unlock and the block, and the wake-up would be lost.
distractors: So the mutex can never be held by two threads.
So Broadcast wakes threads in FIFO order.
So the waiting thread keeps its priority.

cards.question: Birrell: how many waiting threads does Signal wake?
cards.answer: At least one (it may wake more).
cards.memory: One reason the condition must be re-checked in a WHILE loop.
distractors: Exactly one, always.
All of them.
None until the mutex is unlocked.

cards.question: Birrell: what is an alert?
cards.answer: A request asking a thread to abandon a long wait or computation.
distractors: A signal from the kernel that a device finished I/O.
A warning that a deadlock was detected.
A condition variable that wakes all waiters.

cards.question: Birrell: AlertWait vs TestAlert?
cards.answer: AlertWait is a Wait that raises Alerted if the thread is alerted; TestAlert just polls whether it was alerted.
distractors: AlertWait polls; TestAlert blocks until alerted.
AlertWait alerts another thread; TestAlert alerts itself.
Both block; AlertWait also releases the mutex.

cards.question: Birrell: what does a mutex really protect?
cards.answer: An invariant on the shared data that holds whenever the mutex is unlocked.
distractors: A single variable, nothing more.
The code, not the data.
The CPU that runs the critical section.

cards.question: Birrell: what must you do before calling Wait?
cards.answer: Restore the mutex's invariant, because Wait releases the mutex and other threads will see the data.
distractors: Unlock the mutex yourself.
Signal every other condition variable.
Nothing; Wait saves the data for you.

cards.question: Birrell's race: table[i] := r; i := i + 1 without a mutex. What goes wrong?
cards.answer: Two threads interleave: one entry is lost (overwritten) and a slot is orphaned.
distractors: Deadlock: both threads wait forever.
Nothing; each statement is atomic.
The table grows twice as fast.

cards.question: Birrell: how do you prevent deadlock between mutexes?
cards.answer: Impose a partial order on lock acquisition (always lock in that order).
distractors: Use one condition variable per mutex.
Always use Broadcast instead of Signal.
Give every thread the same priority.

cards.question: What is the lock granularity trade-off?
cards.answer: Finer-grained locks mean fewer conflicts but more complexity.
cards.memory: Birrell's example: one global lock for the file table plus one lock per open file.
distractors: Finer locks mean more conflicts but simpler code.
Coarser locks mean fewer conflicts and more parallelism.
Granularity only affects memory use.

cards.question: What is priority inversion?
cards.answer: Low-priority C holds mutex M, medium-priority B runs, and high-priority A, blocked on M, waits behind B.
distractors: A high-priority thread starves all low-priority ones.
Two threads each hold a lock the other needs.
The scheduler runs threads in reverse priority order.

cards.question: What fixes priority inversion?
cards.answer: Priority inheritance: the lock holder temporarily runs at the blocked waiter's priority.
cards.memory: Birrell described the problem (SRC didn't solve it); Eykholt's SunOS kernel solved it with priority inheritance plus turnstiles.
distractors: Lock ordering.
Using Broadcast instead of Signal.
Adaptive mutexes.

cards.question: Birrell: when is an unlocked read (double-checked initialization) safe?
cards.answer: Only as a "hint", and only if the language guarantees it.
distractors: Always, since reads never change data.
Never, under any circumstances.
Whenever the variable is an integer.

cards.question: Birrell's term: what is a "spurious wakeup" in the readers/writer example?
cards.answer: Waking threads that can't proceed; fixed by using separate condition variables for readers and writers.
cards.memory: Terminology trap: the lecture's "spurious wake-up" is what Birrell calls a spurious lock conflict.
distractors: A woken thread blocking on the mutex the signaler still holds; fixed by signaling after unlocking.

cards.question: Birrell's term: what is a "spurious lock conflict"?
cards.answer: A woken thread immediately blocks on the mutex that the signaler still holds.
cards.memory: This is what the lecture calls a spurious wake-up.
distractors: Two threads locking mutexes in opposite order.

cards.answer: Signal after the LOCK clause ends (after unlocking), so the woken thread doesn't block on the mutex.
distractors: Use separate condition variables for readers and writers.
Replace Wait with a spin loop.

cards.answer: Count waiting writers, and make new readers wait while any writer is waiting.
distractors: Give writers their own mutex.
Use Signal for readers and Broadcast for writers.

cards.question: Birrell: what did the readers/writer fixes cost, and what's his advice?
cards.answer: The code grew from 15 to 30 lines; add fixes only if the load actually needs them.
distractors: They halved throughput; always skip them.
Nothing; always add them.

cards.question: What is the nested monitor problem?
cards.answer: A thread waits on monitor b while still holding monitor a's mutex, so the thread that would signal it (which needs a) deadlocks.
distractors: A monitor that calls itself recursively.

A signal handler that locks a mutex.

cards.question: Birrell: how are pipeline stages connected?
cards.answer: By producer-consumer queues (e.g., PaintChar → Rasterize → Painter).
distractors: By shared global variables with no locks.
By Join on each previous stage.
By signals between processes.

cards.answer: The number of stages (and the stages must be balanced).
distractors: The number of CPUs only.
The length of the queues.
The number of mutexes.

cards.answer: Extra runnable threads hurt performance; blocked threads are cheap.
distractors: Both are free.

cards.answer: A Fork costs about 2–3 scheduling decisions, which outweighs a tiny task.
distractors: Fork copies the whole address space.

cards.answer: Block only the calling thread, not the whole process.

distractors: Block every thread in the process.

cards.answer: A lower layer calling up into a higher one (e.g., network receive), avoiding a context switch per layer.
distractors: A system call from user mode to the kernel.
A thread raising its own priority.
A signal sent to the parent process.

cards.answer: Don't hold a mutex while up-calling.
distractors: Always hold every mutex while up-calling.
Disable interrupts while up-calling.

cards.question: Birrell: what are version stamps for?
cards.answer: Detecting stale cached data.
distractors: Ordering lock acquisition.
Numbering threads for Join.
Tracking which CPU a thread ran on.

cards.question: Birrell: what is a work crew?
cards.answer: A fixed pool of threads processing a queue of requests.

distractors: A chain of stages, one thread per stage.

cards.question: Birrell: what four properties should threaded programs aim for?
cards.answer: Useful, correct, live, efficient (get it correct first, then fast).
distractors: Fast, small, portable, secure.
Lock-free, wait-free, fair, simple.
Correct, fast, cheap, parallel.

cards.question: Birrell: how should library entry points behave?
cards.answer: Thread-safe and synchronous.
distractors: Asynchronous with callbacks.
Single-threaded only.
Lock-free and non-blocking.

cards.question: What are the limits of Birrell's paper?
cards.answer: A tutorial with no experiments; selective and biased toward SRC's design; Modula-2+ examples not meant for production.
distractors: Simulation only, with synthetic workloads.
Uniprocessor only, with small memory.
No end-to-end benchmarks; assumes interrupts rarely block.

cards.question: Eykholt et al. (1992): what did they do to SunOS 5.0 (Solaris 2.0)?
cards.answer: Rebuilt the kernel around kernel threads, making it fully preemptible, real-time capable, and SMP-ready.
distractors: Added a user-level threads library on top of the old kernel.

cards.answer: SMP concurrency, multiple threads per user process, and bounded real-time dispatch latency.
distractors: Portability, security, and smaller memory use.
Faster I/O, faster file systems, and faster networking.

cards.question: SunOS: what is a kernel thread?
cards.answer: The unit scheduled onto a CPU: just a small struct plus a stack.
distractors: A full process with its own address space.

cards.question: SunOS: what is an LWP?

distractors: A kernel thread with no user process.

cards.answer: Every LWP has a kernel thread, but not every kernel thread has an LWP.

distractors: Every kernel thread has an LWP, but not every LWP has a kernel thread.

distractors: Per-user, per-group, per-session, per-terminal.

cards.answer: Per-LWP data (user registers) is swappable; per-kernel-thread data (kernel registers) is not.
distractors: Per-kernel-thread is swappable; per-LWP is not.
Both are swappable.
Neither is swappable.

cards.question: SPARC register %g7: what does it point to in the kernel vs in user space?
cards.answer: Kernel: the current kernel thread (curthread). User space: the current user thread's TLS.
distractors: Kernel: the current process. User space: the stack pointer.
Kernel: the interrupt table. User space: the heap.
Both: the current CPU's run queue.

cards.question: SunOS: what are the three scheduling classes?
cards.answer: System, timesharing, and real-time.
distractors: Batch, interactive, and idle.
FIFO, round-robin, and lottery.
Kernel, user, and interrupt.

cards.question: SunOS: when is kernel preemption turned off?
cards.answer: Only in small, bounded sections.
distractors: Whenever any mutex is held.
For the whole time a system call runs.

cards.question: Why does an adaptive mutex spin only while the lock owner is running?
cards.answer: A running owner (on another CPU) will likely release soon; a sleeping owner won't, so spinning would waste the CPU.
distractors: Spinning is only allowed in user mode.
A running owner can't be preempted.

cards.question: SunOS: which locks get priority inheritance, and why those?
cards.answer: Mutexes and writer locks, because they have a single owner to boost.
distractors: Reader locks, because they have many owners.
Condition variables, because they have waiters.
Spin locks, because they never sleep.

cards.question: SunOS: what is a turnstile?
cards.answer: A per-lock structure holding the sleep queue and priority-inheritance info; more predictable than hashed sleep queues.
distractors: A spin lock used only by interrupt handlers.
A queue of runnable threads per CPU.

cards.question: Interrupts as threads: what does "pinned" mean?
cards.answer: The interrupted thread is pinned (held in place, can't run elsewhere) while the interrupt thread borrows its CPU.
distractors: The interrupt thread is bound to one LWP forever.

cards.answer: Only if its handler blocks.
distractors: On every interrupt.
Only for timer interrupts.
Only when the interrupted thread is idle.

cards.question: SunOS: what is special about interrupts above "thread level"?
cards.answer: They are not handled as threads and may use only spin locks.
distractors: They always become full threads.
They may block on any mutex.
They are ignored.

cards.question: SunOS: about how much memory does each interrupt thread use?
cards.answer: About 8 KB.
distractors: About 1.7 KB.
About 1 MB.
About 128 MB.

cards.question: What are the limits of the Eykholt (SunOS kernel) paper?
cards.answer: No end-to-end benchmarks; the net-gain argument assumes interrupts rarely block; deadlock detection misses reader locks and condition variables.
distractors: No experiments at all; a biased tutorial.
Simulation only, with synthetic workloads.
Uniprocessor only, with simulated WAN conditions.

cards.question: Stein & Shah (1992): what problem did they address?
cards.answer: One LWP per thread wastes kernel resources, since most threads are idle at any moment.
distractors: The kernel couldn't be preempted.
Web servers blocked on disk I/O.
Multithreaded cores left the pipeline idle.

cards.question: Stein & Shah: what is their solution?
cards.answer: A user-level library that multiplexes many cheap threads onto a small, self-adjusting pool of LWPs (M:N).
distractors: One kernel thread per user thread (1:1).
All user threads on a single LWP (M:1).

cards.answer: A thread permanently tied to one LWP, giving system-wide scheduling scope (e.g., for real-time).
distractors: A thread that shares the LWP pool with others.
A thread that can't be preempted by signals.
A thread whose stack size is fixed.

distractors: A thread permanently tied to one LWP.
A thread with no stack.

distractors: In the kernel's LWP struct; it holds the signal mask.

distractors: New, ready, running, waiting, terminated.

distractors: Round-robin with a kernel timer per thread.

distractors: Idling: a thread sleeps on a mutex. Parking: an LWP is destroyed.
